newsitem.title: USA: Sanctions block U.S. firms from $790 bln market.
newsitem.headline: Sanctions block U.S. firms from $790 bln market.

text.p: U.S. sanctions against 35 countries over the last four years have cut off or limited American companies' access to $790 billion worth of markets, the National Association of Manufacturers said Tuesday.

"The sanctioned countries represent 2.3 billion potential consumers of U.S. goods and services (42 percent of the world's population) and $790 billion worth of export markets (19 percent of the world's total," the group said in a report.
The list of potential lost markets includes countries against which the U.S. has invoked sanctions, but not imposed a trade embargo, such as Canada and Mexico.

But the report did not include countries that might retaliate against the U.S. move last year to punish foreign firms that invest in oil and gas in Iran and Libya, which the group said would hit most of Europe, Latin America and Japan.

Few attempts have been made to assess the impact unilateral economic sanctions on U.S. employment and exports, the association said in its "Catalog of New U.S. Unilateral Economic Sanctions for Foreign Policy Purposes 1993-96".
A two year old study by the Council on Competitiveness looking at eight cases found that $6 billion in export sales and 120,000 jobs had been put at risk.

Although many of the countries targeted by Washington's policies were still open to trade with the United States, the manufacturers' group said that even limited sanctions made those countries wary of doing business with U.S. firms.

"The catalog illustrates the dangers of what former Secretary of State George Schultz called 'light-switch diplomacy,' the belief that ... major commercial relationships can be turned on and off like a light," the report said.
The group highlighted U.S. laws that ban nuclear electric exports to China, which has a need for $20 billion worth of nuclear power generating equipment.

The report said Chinese leaders have been reluctant to let U.S. companies in on major power projects. "They fear that over the course of the project's life, U.S. trade with China will become hostage to U.S. politics," it said.

The report also highlighted the souring of relations between Washington and its allies in Europe and Canada as a result of the Helms-Burton law, which targeted foreign investors who benefited from property confiscated by the Cuban government.
The association urged the U.S. government to avoid unilateral sanctions and attempt to use diplomatic, political and military measures to isolate problem countries.

The group pressed the government to assess annually the impact of its unilateral sanctions on the targeted government and on U.S. companies, allow sanctions to lapse after two years unless Congress approves them, and let the President end sanctions if it is in the national interest.
